summary: A 1974 proposal for extending the ARPANET host-to-host protocol so that hosts can detect and recover from lost messages. It builds on earlier discussion in RFC 534, RFC 516, RFC 512, RFC 492 and RFC 467.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 663 proposes a way for network hosts to notice missing messages and coordinate a response. Hosts can retransmit, negotiate whether to accept a loss, or close a connection if recovery is not possible.

subtitle: A proposed Host-to-Host extension for detecting lost messages and coordinating recovery.

tldr.problem: The existing Host-to-Host protocol did not provide a general way to detect lost messages or recover from them, which could leave hosts with inconsistent connection state.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal uses a four-bit Message Sequence Number and an eight-bit Link Resynch Number, plus control messages for reporting loss, requesting status and coordinating retransmission or closure.
tldr.outcome: Type B hosts can use the extension with each other while simulating Type A behavior with hosts that have not adopted it.

today: The unit records RFC 663's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It proposes an extension to the Host-to-Host protocol for lost-message detection and recovery.

sections.title: Detecting Lost Host-to-Host Messages
sections.content:
The RFC says the existing Host-to-Host protocol does not provide for detecting lost messages, detecting data errors or recovering from those problems. A lost control message can leave the two hosts with different views of a connection; the “lost allocate” problem can prevent a sender from transmitting more messages.

RFC 663 proposes an extension for lost-message detection and orderly recovery. It does not itself add a general method for detecting errors in the data, though the author expects the recovery procedures could apply if such detection were added.
sections.plainLanguage: If a control message disappears, two hosts can disagree about the connection and stop communicating. This proposal gives them a way to detect missing messages and coordinate what happens next.

sections.title: Sequence and Resynchronization Numbers
sections.content:
The proposal uses the four unused bits in the message-id as a Message Sequence Number (MSN), with values from 1 through 15 and then back to 1. A receiver can detect a gap in this sequence. Zero indicates that the sender is not using the proposed detection and recovery protocol.

An eight-bit Link Resynch Number (LRN) identifies the current resynchronization state for a link. On detecting a missing message, the receiver advances its LRN and reports the first missing MSN. The RFC notes that a sequence of exactly 15 lost messages could defeat simple gap detection, and describes status exchange to help prevent that case.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message carries a small sequence number. If the receiver sees a later number with a gap, it knows messages may be missing and uses the resynchronization number to coordinate recovery.

sections.title: Recovery and Control Messages
sections.content:
The receiver reports loss with an LMR (Lost Message from Receiver) command naming the link, new LRN and first missing MSN. The sender may retransmit from that point. If it cannot retransmit on a regular connection, it may send LMS (Lost Message from Sender) with a count of lost messages; the receiver can close the connection or accept the loss with LMA.

For a control link, an unrecoverable loss requires a reset and reinitialization rather than accepting missing control messages. The RFC also defines status queries and replies so a sender can learn what the receiver has received and decide when to free stored messages. A lost control message may be retransmitted with the same sequence values, and the receiver may ignore duplicates.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver tells the sender where the gap begins. The sender can resend from there, ask whether the receiver will accept missing data, or close the connection if it cannot recover.

sections.title: Compatibility Between Host Types
sections.content:
The RFC calls hosts that do not adopt the extension Type A and hosts that do Type B. Type A hosts use zero for MSN and LRN. Type B hosts use the new procedures when communicating with another Type B host and simulate Type A behavior when communicating with a Type A host.

The proposal lets hosts choose recovery behavior suited to their capabilities, while requiring consistent protocol behavior. The concluding remarks state that partial recovery is not appropriate for every use; for example, the RFC expects file transfer to require an abort after an irrecoverable error.
sections.plainLanguage: Older hosts keep using zero values. A host with the new protocol can recognize that and behave compatibly, while using recovery procedures with another upgraded host.
